title: Too Much on One Desk
objective: Allocate team workload by risk value and capacity, and protect the team from burnout.
subject: Your team, your call
briefing: You now lead three analysts. Requests are piling up faster than the team can deliver. Decide what gets done this month and what doesn't, and tell stakeholders.

documents.title: Team capacity this month
documents.body: Three analysts, about 10 days each = 30 analyst-days. {sh:analyst} is already at 120% and has asked for help. One analyst is new and needs supervision.

steps.prompt: Choose which requests the team takes on this month (capacity 30 analyst-days).
steps.hint: Maximise risk value within 30 days. Low-value items can be declined or deferred.

steps.prompt: {sh:analyst} is at 120% and asking for help. What do you do?

options.text: Take two of their tasks off them this month, agree priorities in a 1:1, and check workload weekly.
Ask them to push through; it's a busy month.
options.feedback: Sustained overload leads to errors and burnout.

options.text: Do their work yourself at night.
options.feedback: Unsustainable and hides the capacity problem.

steps.prompt: Commercial insists their launch assessment is urgent and threatens to escalate. You haven't scheduled it this month. Response?

options.text: Explain the priorities and the capacity, offer a scoped 3-day rapid review of the top risks now, and the full assessment next month.
options.feedback: Shows trade-offs transparently and offers a proportionate option.

options.text: Drop the fraud investigation to fit it in.
Refuse and let them escalate.

steps.prompt: How do you develop the new analyst while delivering?

options.text: Pair them on the cyber control test with clear checkpoints and a worked example from last quarter.
Give them the archive task to keep them busy.
Let them shadow without contributing.

debrief.summary: You allocated scarce capacity to the highest-value work and protected your team.
key_points: Prioritise by risk value per day.
Workload is a risk to quality.
debrief.stronger_approach: Publish the queue and the rationale monthly so stakeholders see trade-offs before they escalate.
debrief.transfer: Every leadership role is an allocation problem: budget, people and attention.

endings.title: Strong outcome
endings.text: Your work set a high standard. Stakeholders now come to you early.

endings.title: Adequate outcome
endings.text: Solid work with gaps. Your manager asks you to revisit one or two points.

endings.title: Needs rework
endings.text: The work needs another pass. Use the debrief and try again when ready.

title: Reviewing Junior Work
objective: Review an analyst's assessment for technical errors and give feedback that builds capability.
subject: Could you review my assessment?
briefing: Here's my first assessment of the warehouse fire risk. I'm not very confident about it. Could you review it before it goes to the COO?

documents.title: Draft assessment
documents.body:
Risk: Fire.
Inherent: likelihood 2, impact 5. Residual: likelihood 1, impact 2.
Controls: sprinklers (last tested 3 years ago), fire alarms, staff training (60% completed).
Expected loss: 2 x 5 = 10, so about {m:10000}.
Recommendation: risk is low, no action needed.

steps.prompt: Which errors does the draft contain?

options.text: Risk statement lacks cause and consequence
Residual impact drops from 5 to 2 although sprinklers are untested
options.why: Untested controls cannot justify a three-step reduction.

options.text: Expected loss calculated by multiplying ordinal scores
Inherent likelihood of 2 is unreasonable
options.why: Plausible for a warehouse with standard precautions.

steps.prompt: How do you deliver the feedback?

options.text: Meet in person: start with what's good, walk through each issue with the reason, and ask them to revise using a worked example.
Return it with tracked changes and no discussion.
options.feedback: Efficient but misses the teaching moment.

options.text: Rewrite it yourself and send it to the COO.

steps.prompt: What residual rating would you expect, given untested sprinklers and incomplete training?
steps.hint: Rate inherent first, then credit only controls with evidence.
steps.why: Inherent L2 x I5 is plausible, but the inherent impact of a major warehouse fire is better rated 4 here given the site's size; residual stays near inherent because the corrective control (sprinklers) is untested.

steps.prompt: Write two coaching points for the analyst.
steps.model_answer: Your control list is a good start. First, only credit controls we have evidence for: sprinklers untested for three years can't justify cutting impact from 5 to 2. Second, ratings are ordinal, so 2 x 5 isn't money: use probability ranges and loss estimates for expected loss.

debrief.summary: You found the technical errors and turned them into learning.
key_points: Review for logic, evidence and method.
Feedback should teach the principle behind each correction.
debrief.stronger_approach: Build a short checklist for the team covering the common errors you found.
debrief.transfer: Reviewing others' work is the core of every supervisory role, from audit to engineering.

endings.title: Strong outcome
endings.text: Your work set a high standard. Stakeholders now come to you early.

endings.title: Adequate outcome
endings.text: Solid work with gaps. Your manager asks you to revisit one or two points.

endings.title: Needs rework
endings.text: The work needs another pass. Use the debrief and try again when ready.

title: Pushback from Operations
objective: Resolve stakeholder disagreement over overdue actions and escalate proportionately.
subject: Your team keeps chasing my managers
briefing: Your analysts keep chasing my managers about overdue actions. We are running a business here. I want it to stop.

documents.title: Escalation policy
documents.body: Actions on risks with residual score 15+ overdue by 3+ months must be reported to the executive risk committee.

steps.prompt: How do you open the conversation with {sh:coo}?

options.text: Acknowledge the pressure, propose one consolidated monthly check-in instead of ad hoc chasing, and focus on the one action that must be escalated.
options.feedback: Reduces friction and keeps what matters.

options.text: Tell them the policy requires chasing.
Agree to stop chasing.

steps.prompt: The induction-system action (residual 15, 4 months overdue, 'no budget') meets the escalation criteria. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the COO you must report it, offer to present it jointly with the budget ask, and propose an interim manual induction check.
options.feedback: Transparent escalation with a constructive path.

options.text: Leave it out of the report to preserve the relationship.
options.feedback: Breaches policy and hides a material risk.

options.text: Escalate without telling the COO.

steps.prompt: Rank the three actions by urgency.
steps.why: Rank by residual risk and time overdue.

steps.prompt: The forklift supplier delay is genuine. What's the right response?

options.text: Agree a revised date, add an interim control (speed signage and spot checks), and record the reason.
Mark it overdue and escalate.
options.feedback: Escalation adds little when the cause is outside the owner's control.

options.text: Close it.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Agree a revised date, add an interim control (speed signage and spot checks), and record the reason.”

debrief.summary: You kept oversight while reducing friction, and escalated what policy required.
debrief.stronger_approach: Show the COO the trend in their area's overdue actions compared with peers.
debrief.transfer: Navigating owners' pushback is the same with project sponsors, IT and clinicians.

endings.text: Your work set a high standard. Stakeholders now come to you early.

endings.title: Adequate outcome

title: Drawing the Line: Risk Appetite
objective: Turn vague appetite statements into measurable metrics with tolerances and escalation.
subject: Make our appetite statement mean something
briefing: Our appetite statement says we have a 'low appetite for operational disruption'. The board asked what that means in practice. Fix it.

documents.title: Current appetite statement
documents.body:
- Low appetite for operational disruption.
- Moderate appetite for innovation.
- No appetite for safety incidents.

steps.prompt: Which properties should an appetite metric have?

options.text: Measurable and linked to a statement
A threshold for appetite and a wider tolerance
A named owner and escalation route
Wording broad enough to avoid breaches

steps.prompt: Which is the best rewrite of 'low appetite for operational disruption'?

options.text: No more than 2 outages over 4 hours a year and none over 8 hours (appetite); 4 outages or any over 24 hours triggers board escalation (tolerance).
We will minimise disruption at all times.
Zero outages.
options.feedback: Measurable but unrealistic; it will be breached constantly and ignored.

steps.prompt: 'No appetite for safety incidents' - what's the issue?

options.text: Zero appetite is right for serious harm, but stated as 'no incidents' it may discourage reporting; express it as no tolerance for avoidable serious harm, with leading metrics.
options.feedback: Keeps the ethical intent and avoids perverse incentives.

options.text: None; zero is ambitious.
options.feedback: Ambition is fine; incentives to hide minor incidents are not.

options.text: Raise it to 'low appetite'.

steps.prompt: Last year had 3 outages over 4 hours against the proposed appetite of 2. By what percentage was appetite exceeded?
{sh:cco} worries measurable appetite will 'tie our hands'. Response?

options.text: Explain that clear limits speed up decisions inside them and show where we have moderate appetite for innovation.
options.feedback: Appetite enables as well as constrains.

options.text: Tell them it's a board requirement.
options.feedback: This addresses part of the problem but misses something important. A stronger option was: “Explain that clear limits speed up decisions inside them and show where we have moderate appetite for innovation.”

options.text: Agree to keep it vague.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Explain that clear limits speed up decisions inside them and show where we have moderate appetite for innovation.”

debrief.summary: You converted vague intentions into measurable, tiered appetite.
key_points: Appetite needs metrics, tolerances and owners.
debrief.stronger_approach: Back-test the new metrics against the last three years to see how often they would have triggered.
debrief.transfer: Appetite frameworks underpin bank capital planning, hospital safety governance and infrastructure investment.

endings.text: Your work set a high standard. Stakeholders now come to you early.

title: Budget Defender
objective: Allocate a constrained risk budget for maximum risk reduction and defend it to the CFO.
subject: Your budget is being cut by 20%
briefing: Your treatment budget for next year is {m:500000}, down from {m:625000}. Tell me what you'll fund and what we're giving up.

steps.prompt: Select treatments within {m:500000} to maximise risk reduction.
steps.hint: Compare reduction per unit of cost. Value here = annual EL reduction in thousands.

steps.prompt: What is the ratio of annual EL reduction to cost for MFA?
The CFO asks: 'Why not just buy the GRC software? Everyone has one.'

options.text: It mainly improves efficiency ({m:40000} reduction for {m:250000}); funding it would displace MFA or dual-sourcing, which reduce far more risk.
options.feedback: Opportunity cost framed in the CFO's terms.

options.text: Agree; it will make us look mature.
Say risk software isn't your decision.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “It mainly improves efficiency ({m:40000} reduction for {m:250000}); funding it would displace MFA or dual-sourcing, which reduce far more risk.”

steps.prompt: State what you are giving up and why, in two sentences.
steps.model_answer: We are deferring the GRC software and executive training because they reduce far less risk per unit of cost than MFA, dual-sourcing, fire door devices and fraud automation. We accept that register administration stays manual next year and will revisit when budget allows.

debrief.summary: You maximised risk reduction within a cut budget and explained the opportunity cost.
key_points: Rank by reduction per unit cost, then check non-financial factors.
Say clearly what you are not doing.
debrief.stronger_approach: Show the CFO the residual risk profile with and without the cut.
debrief.transfer: Every budget round is an allocation under constraint.

title: Challenging the Business
objective: Challenge a business decision constructively using evidence, options and appropriate escalation.
subject: Maintenance is being cut again
briefing: Operations plans to cut the planned maintenance budget by 25% to hit the cost target. Our asset failure risk is already above appetite. You need to challenge this. Carefully.

documents.title: Maintenance proposal
documents.body: Cut planned maintenance by 25% ({m:1200000} saving). Move to run-to-failure for non-critical assets. Approved in principle by {sh:coo} and {sh:cfo}.

rows: Engineers' estimate: extra failures if cut

steps.prompt: What is the expected cost of the extra failures per year (4 x {m:260000})?
How do you approach {sh:coo}?

options.text: Share the failure data privately, acknowledge the cost target, and propose a targeted cut that protects critical assets.
Write to the CEO that the COO is putting the business at risk.
Accept it; it's approved.
options.feedback: Approval in principle is when challenge is most useful.

steps.prompt: The COO agrees to protect critical assets but still wants a 15% cut, which keeps asset risk just above appetite. What next?

options.text: Record the residual risk above appetite and ask the executive committee to accept it formally or fund the gap.
options.feedback: Right route: an authorised decision, recorded.

options.text: Re-score the risk so it fits appetite.
Accept on the COO's authority.

steps.prompt: Write a short challenge note to the executive committee.
steps.model_answer: The proposed 25% maintenance cut saves {m:1200000} but engineers expect four more critical failures a year, costing about {m:1040000}. A targeted 15% cut protecting critical assets saves less but keeps failures near current levels; residual risk remains just above appetite. We ask the committee to either accept that residual risk formally or fund the gap.

debrief.summary: You challenged with evidence, offered an alternative and routed the residual decision correctly.
key_points: Above-appetite risk needs explicit authorised acceptance.
debrief.stronger_approach: Track the maintenance backlog KRI monthly and pre-agree what happens if it crosses warning.
debrief.transfer: Constructive challenge is the core of the second-line role in every industry.

title: Leadership Capstone: The Overdue Audit
objective: Demonstrate first-leadership competence: lead a team through competing demands, manage stakeholders, allocate budget and escalate correctly.
subject: Capstone: unsatisfactory audit opinion
briefing: Internal audit has rated risk management 'unsatisfactory'. You have six weeks to agree a credible remediation plan with management, using your team and budget.

rows: 34% of risk actions overdue, some by over a year
Control ratings not supported by testing
Risk appetite not used in decisions
Register not reviewed by owners in 9 months

documents.title: Resources
documents.body: Team: you and 3 analysts. Remediation budget: {m:150000}. Executive committee meets in four weeks.

steps.prompt: Choose remediation options within {m:150000}.
Your analysts are already stretched. How do you staff the plan?

options.text: Assign each analyst a finding to own end-to-end, pause low-value reporting for six weeks, and run a weekly 30-minute check-in.
Ask everyone to work longer hours.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Assign each analyst a finding to own end-to-end, pause low-value reporting for six weeks, and run a weekly 30-minute check-in.”

options.text: Do it all yourself.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Assign each analyst a finding to own end-to-end, pause low-value reporting for six weeks, and run a weekly 30-minute check-in.”

steps.prompt: A director argues their overdue actions should be 'reset' with new dates and no record of the delay. Response?

options.text: Agree realistic new dates but keep the history visible; audit and the committee need to see the trend.
Reset them; a clean start helps morale.
Refuse any new dates.

steps.prompt: What do you present to the executive committee?

options.text: Root causes behind the findings, the funded plan with owners and dates, what remains outside appetite, and the decisions needed from them.
A list of every overdue action.
An argument that audit was too harsh.

steps.prompt: Write the opening paragraph of your committee paper.
steps.model_answer: Internal audit rated risk management unsatisfactory. The root causes are unclear ownership of actions, control ratings without testing, and appetite that is not used in decisions. Our plan funds a control testing programme, owner workshops and appetite checks in investment papers, with named owners and dates over six weeks. We ask the committee to approve the plan and to hold owners to the revised dates.

debrief.summary: You led the team, allocated scarce budget and kept governance honest under pressure.
key_points: Keep history visible when resetting dates.
Bring decisions, not lists, to committees.
debrief.stronger_approach: Agree with audit up front what evidence will close each finding.
debrief.transfer: Remediation leadership is the same for regulatory findings, safety notices and project recoveries.
